analysis: A coherent related-fields response follows religion in visual culture, narratives, historical material and political life. World Myth & Literature, World Archaeology, African Art & Heritage, Renaissance Italy and Heritage & Ancient Democracy supply actual traditions, narratives, religious material culture and specific relationships between belief and institutions. Introduction to Western Art History brings direct visual interpretation and the role of religious change. Philosophy, rights, social inquiry and political conflict contribute analytical perspectives. Museums and art historiography contribute interpretation and research rather than religious field methods. Specialist coverage of Christianity, Judaism, Islam, South Asian religions, ritual and religion-specific research remains a material gap, shown explicitly and flagged in caution mode.

ACCPPDE101.name: Personal & Professional Development
ACCPPDE101.contribution: Academic writing, evidence use, argument and reflection underpin historical and social inquiry.

GOSGATE102.name: Law, Society & Justice
GOSGATE102.contribution: establishes how law, social institutions and justice interact, providing a foundation for studying religious freedom and religion in public life without claiming specialist religion law

GOSLAWJ111.name: Human Rights: Law & Philosophy
GOSLAWJ111.contribution: studies human-rights law and its historical-philosophical foundations, including natural-law traditions, as a concrete basis for freedom of religion and speech questions

GOSLAWJ213.name: Comparative Constitutional Law
GOSLAWJ213.contribution: compares constitutional institutions, fundamental rights and remedies across jurisdictions, providing legal tools for questions of freedom and public authority

GOSPHIL111.name: Introduction to Western Philosophy

GOSPHIL212.name: Ethics
GOSPHIL212.contribution: develops moral reasoning through major ethical theories and applied problems, supporting the target's religion-and-ethics questions without being relabelled comparative religious ethics

GOSPHIL214.name: Philosophy of Mind
GOSPHIL214.contribution: compares accounts of self and consciousness, including Buddhist approaches, providing a specific cross-traditional philosophical contribution rather than a survey of Buddhism

GOSPOLI111.name: Introduction to Political Philosophy
GOSPOLI111.contribution: provides concepts of authority, liberty, justice and political obligation needed to analyse religious claims and political order

GOSPOLI313.name: Peace & Conflict
GOSPOLI313.contribution: uses legal, political, historical and social perspectives on conflict, identity and peacebuilding to contextualise religion-and-conflict questions

GOSSOCI111.name: Introduction to Sociology
GOSSOCI111.contribution: introduces sociological theory, institutions and race/gender/class analysis for examining belief communities and social identity; it is not presented as sociology of religion

GOSSOCI212.name: Qualitative Research Methodology
GOSSOCI212.contribution: teaches qualitative research design, interpretation and reflexivity for investigating lived meanings and communities without claiming religion-specific ethnography

GOSSOCI311.name: New Issues in Contemporary Social Theory
GOSSOCI311.contribution: studies civil society, solidarity, public spheres and migrant inclusion through theory and an organisation-based project, supporting religion, migration and public-life questions

HCBPSYC111.name: Social Psychology
HCBPSYC111.contribution: examines how social contexts, groups and norms shape beliefs and behaviour, providing a psychological lens on identity without substituting for psychology of religion

HCBPSYC315.name: Youth Resilience to Extremism
HCBPSYC315.contribution: studies youth radicalisation and educational prevention through protective factors, belonging and school climate; this supports the interest in extremism without presuming a religious cause

MCCHEAM111.name: Introduction to Western Art History
MCCHEAM111.contribution: studies how religious and other social changes shape Western visual art and develops close visual analysis of paintings

MCCHEAM112.name: Introduction to World Archaeology
MCCHEAM112.contribution: examines religious, social and gendered identities through ancient material culture across several world regions

MCCHEAM211.name: African Art & Heritage
MCCHEAM211.contribution: studies how western-African visual forms embody religious and social meaning and addresses their museum and colonial histories

MCCHEAM212.name: Renaissance Italy & Global Mediterranean
MCCHEAM212.contribution: studies Renaissance art and architecture in exchange with Islamic courts and wider Mediterranean cultures, supplying a specific historical cross-cultural perspective

MCCHEAM312.name: Modern Art & Modern Museums
MCCHEAM312.contribution: analyses how museums and curatorial strategies shape public interpretation of art, complementing religious visual-heritage questions without assuming religion-specific exhibits

MCCHEAM315.name: Heritage & Ancient Democracy
MCCHEAM315.contribution: directly examines how Athenian democracy was intertwined with myth and religion and expressed through art, literature and architecture

MCCHEAM316.name: Writing Art's Histories
MCCHEAM316.contribution: develops art-historical interpretation, visual analysis and academic writing for studying meaning and identity in religious images and heritage; the methods remain art-historical rather than religious-studies methods

MCCLITR112.name: Great Literary Works
MCCLITR112.contribution: traces themes of mortality, duty and community in epic, tragedy and confessional writing, developing textual interpretation relevant to narratives of belief

MCCLITR211.name: World Myth & Literature
MCCLITR211.contribution: compares mythic narrative traditions including Indian, Greek, Byzantine and Arabic material and their transmission through text, image, orality and performance

MCCMEDI311.name: Media & Race
MCCMEDI311.contribution: studies storytelling, power, race and systemic exclusion through media production, supplying a specific identity-and-representation lens without treating race as religion

alignment.rationale: Both interpret narratives and their transmission. UCR studies myth in literature and other media; Groningen explicitly studies the use of religious texts.
Both interpret visual forms with religious meaning. UCR focuses on African visual and heritage traditions; Groningen studies religious images through iconography.
Both study how religion and politics shape one another. UCR concentrates on Athenian democracy, myth and ritual; Groningen also considers modern politics, conflict and peacebuilding.
Both develop philosophical analysis of belief and questions about God. UCR is a wider introduction to philosophy.
Both teach ethical reasoning. Groningen combines religion, ethics and care; UCR studies more general ethical theories and applications.
UCR qualitative methodology is useful for community inquiry, but it is not a sufficiently direct counterpart to the comparator's religion-specific research-design course.
The comparator has a dedicated religion-specific thesis-design seminar; no scheduled UCR course reproduces that formation.
The comparator requires a credited 10-EC independent thesis in Religious Studies. UCR optional independent research is shown in parallel but remains outside the scheduled 180 EC.
The comparator's science communication is explicitly about communicating religion research; no scheduled UCR course is a sufficiently direct counterpart.
UCR contains religion-related cultural material but no sustained course in Christianity's history, sources and practice.
General humanities and social-science methods do not reproduce an introduction to the concepts and methods of Religious Studies.
The schedule has qualitative and social inquiry but no course in anthropology of religion.
World Myth & Literature and Philosophy of Mind include Indian or Buddhist material but do not provide a full course in South Asian religions.
No scheduled UCR course provides sustained study of Judaism's history, sources and practice.
General psychology and sociology courses support analysis of belief and identity but do not teach psychology and sociology of religion.
Mediterranean art history includes Islamic courts, but no scheduled UCR course provides sustained study of Islamic history, sources and practice.
No scheduled UCR course provides a sustained theory-and-practice study of religious ritual.
Media & Race supplies an identity-and-power lens, but it does not directly study religion, media and popular culture.
Sociology and social psychology address diversity and identity generally, but not new religious movements or lived religious diversity.
The comparator's genuine 15-EC university or approved personal minor remains visible without invented content.
General sustainability courses were not inserted merely to imitate a religion-and-climate option; the comparator's religious and spiritual framing remains unmatched.
UCR archaeology and environmental study do not reproduce the historical, sociological and spatial analysis of sacred space.
The complete UCR programme addresses selected cultural and political effects through related disciplines, but does not reproduce the comparator's religion-specific specialisation.

academicConstruction: Screened the active workbook names, profiles and descriptions for religion, sacred practice, theology, spiritual care, ritual and religious traditions, then checked complementary heritage, law, psychology, media and research. The Western art course contributes more direct material than Foundations of Comparative Politics, while retained advanced museum and art-history work supports interpretation and keeps six 300-level courses. Heritage & Ancient Democracy is the strongest bounded Religion and Politics alignment through myth, religion and Athenian public institutions. Peace & Conflict adds political and historical tools without assuming a religion syllabus. General sustainability, bioethical and education courses would not sustain the respective specialist religious directions. A second heritage proposal would duplicate the closest composition rather than form a new evidenced direction. Pairwise distinctness is inapplicable to a single accepted option.
